h: Ophelia, the Lady of Shalott and the Turner Prize
p: Some of the most popular paintings in Britain hang here. John Everett Millais's Ophelia shows Shakespeare's tragic heroine floating in a stream surrounded by flowers painted in astonishing detail, and John William Waterhouse's The Lady of Shalott is another visitor favourite. Both belong to a group of artists known as the Pre-Raphaelites, whose bright colours and dreamy stories still pull in the crowds.

Turner's work fills the Clore Gallery, a wing built specially to house the huge collection he left to the nation. Spend some time with his seascapes and storms, which seem to glow from inside. The central Duveen Galleries are used for big sculpture and installation commissions, so there's often something unexpected filling that long, grand space.

The gallery is closely connected with the Turner Prize, one of the best-known and most talked-about contemporary art awards, and the prize exhibition is often shown here, though it also moves around the country in some years. It's a good way to see what younger artists are up to, and it reliably gets people arguing in the best way.

Allow a couple of hours for a relaxed visit. Henry Tate, the sugar merchant who funded the original building, would surely be pleased that it's still free to see the collection. Afterwards, wander the elegant streets of Pimlico, or cross Vauxhall Bridge for a look at the distinctive building of MI6 on the opposite bank.
